https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Police hurt in Bristol riot over right to protest
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
A total of 20 police officers were injured and some feared they would be killed in Bristol last night in a riot that police are describing as the worst case of violent disorder in the city for a decade.
One officer suffered a punctured lung and another a fractured arm as a protest against a proposed law to enhance police powers degenerated into violence in the early evening.
Two police vehicles were set on fire while officers were attacked with fireworks and pelted with bottles in a four-hour stand-off.
Police and witnesses to the violence said that the clashes arose after a peaceful protest involving more than 3,000 people had come to an end.
Andy Roebuck, chairman of the Avon and Somerset Police Federation, said some officers at the riot “thought they would be killed” amid the violence.
Andy Marsh, the chief constable of Avon & Somerset Police, said that it was the worst violence in Bristol since the looting in 2011 that arose after the shooting of Mark Duggan by armed police.
Marsh said that his officers had made seven arrests last night for violent disorder and for possession of an offensive weapon, adding that police will release images of suspected rioters today as they seek to question up to 400 people.
“I don’t believe that what they were doing was protesting against the policing bill, they were there with anti-policie rhetoric, they were there with violence and threats and graffiti and damage and violence,” he told BBC News.
“So there could be as many as 400 people we want too speak to — anyone at that violent scene, after it became violent.”
He said the force will launch one of the biggest appeals for wanted suspects it has ever done and asked the public to help by sending footage of clashes to add to video recorded on cameras worn by officers.
“The cost of policing this operation, carrying out the subsequent investigation and repairing and replacing our vehicles and damage to our city centre station will run into the millions,” he added.
Marsh said his team assessed that the group had been “looking for a trigger to provoke a violent response”.
By 6pm protesters were defacing police vehicles with slogans such as “F*** the pol”, throwing missiles and fireworks at officers, and graffiti was sprayed on the riot shields of officers protecting the entrance to the station.
“Simply wading in and making a handful of arrests from a mob of hundreds of angry people would have left the officers more vulnerable and the station more vulnerable from being overrun,” Marsh told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.
Marsh said three marked police vehicles were set alight and nine vehicles “used for safeguarding the most vulnerable” were also damaged.
Marvin Rees, the elected mayor of Bristol, supported the police response last night and said the group who attacked the police station were “self-indulgent, self-centred people who came here looking for a conflict to take advantage of”.
“We have seen situations where people are looking for a trigger,” he told Today. “You choose the time to move on a crowd and things could have been a lot worse. Images are going to be published and people tracked down and arrested and quite rightly.”
Rees said the rioters were having a “political tantrum” and he “wouldn’t do these people the service of talking about them in the same sentence as the crime bill”.
Reporters on the street yesterday described the initial peaceful protest at College Green as being a “festival-like gathering” with people holding placards, chanting slogans and dancing to music.
People arrived at the green, where a peaceful vigil for Sarah Everard was attended by hundreds of people on March 13, from 2pm yesterday. This was despite lockdown rules preventing people from gathering and police advice to stay away after posters for a Kill The Bill protest, opposing new laws to control the public’s ability to protest, had been circulating on social media.
The police took a light-touch approach to the protest, watching from the sidelines, questioning some people about their presence and attempting to deter people from holding any kind of organised event. However, numbers swelled into the thousands.
A group estimated to be as large as 3,000 people began to move towards the Broadmead shopping district, with the march splitting into two.
Witnesses said the atmosphere remained calm and Avon & Somerset Police continued to monitor the situation, saying in a tweet that “enforcement action will be taken retrospectively when necessary and proportionate”.
Mass gatherings are banned under coronavirus legislation. Many protesters carried placards with slogans such as “Say no to UK police state”.
One group of protesters moved to Castle Park before many dispersed, but the tone of the gathering changed when several hundred gathered at the Bridewell Street police station late in the afternoon.
What began as a sit-down protest outside the station became more confrontational, with anti-police graffiti sprayed on buildings and vehicles and missiles and fireworks hurled at police.
By early evening the station was coming under siege, with people on a rooftop at the front of the building, smashing windows, spraying graffiti and letting off fireworks. Police say several officers were hurt as missiles were thrown.
Officers in riot gear were deployed and lines of officers attempting to split the crowd and keep people back as police vans were attacked.
A group attempted to topple a van and had to be pushed back by officers. The windows of the police station were smashed by people carrying skateboards. The police said no one was able to gain entry.
As night fell the rioters repeatedly clashed with police, setting fire to vehicles and bins and goading police dogs with food.
Many of those involved wore face masks and carried placards with slogans including “Freedom to protest is fundamental to democracy” and “Kill the Bill”.
Ashley George, 25, a bystander, told The Times: “It started kicking off at about 9pm. People were throwing anything they could get their hands on: glass bottles, cartons of milk, stones, bricks. A police car window was smashed and someone set fire to some paper and threw it in. There were no police in it. They had fallen back.”
He added: “It started with vandalism of the police station. Police officers came out with riot shields. They were just doing their jobs. To be honest, they should have used a bit more force than they did.”
Avon & Somerset Police called in extra support from neighbouring forces and deployed more officers in riot gear.
George, who did not take part in the demonstration, said that the troublemakers he spoke to had not been part of the march but had come into the city centre after they heard about the size of the protest. “They were just interested in violence. They were just laughing and joining in.”
Officers with riot shields used a fire extinguisher to put out a blaze under a vehicle. Protesters then set alight a nearby mobile police station van.
A stretch of the M32 motorway was blocked by police to stop people entering the city centre as they continued to deal with the remaining rioters around midnight. It was reopened at about 2am.
Police horse and dog sections were on duty throughout the night and into the early morning.
Priti Patel, the home secretary, said her thoughts were with the injured officers, adding: “Thuggery and disorder by a minority will never be tolerated.”
However, Nadia Whittome, Labour MP for Nottingham East, refused to condemn the Bristol protests during an interview with the BBC’s Politics Live.
She said: “I wish everybody who has been hurt in this a speedy recovery, but I am not going to get in the business of condemning protesters until we know exactly what has happened.”
Challenged, she added that she did not “want to see violence perpetrated against anybody”, but felt that a full investigation is needed both into the protesters and the police actions.
Critics say bill will give police power to stop any protestPriti Patel’s new crime bill will widen the range of conditions police can impose on protests and increase sanctions for those who breach the conditions (Matt Dathan writes).
It will bring static protests in line with marches by allowing the police to impose time limits and maximum noise levels.
The Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill will also give police broader powers to shut down protests that “cause a serious disruption to the running of an organisation”.
Organisers whose protests breach the conditions could face maximum sentences of six months in prison and the maximum fines for people who participate in illegal protests will increase to £2,500.
The Home Office says that the bill is tightly defined to crack down on particular protesting tactics that are designed to cause “unjustifiable disruption” to members of the public.
It was drawn up in direct response to last year’s Extinction Rebellion, Black Lives Matter and anti-HS2 protests.
Examples of the “unjustifiable disruption” given by officials include Extinction Rebellion protesters blocking the passage of an ambulance on emergency calls, glueing themselves to trains during rush hour and blockading printing presses, which prevented 1.5 million newspapers — including copies of The Times — from being distributed last year.
They also pointed to BLM protesters who blocked airport runways that caused delays to hundreds of passengers, and the tunnelling under Euston Square in London, which is preventing the construction of HS2.
Critics of the bill say that it would give police sweeping powers to shut down any protests because the definitions of what constitutes “serious disruption” or a breach of noise levels could be used to deem them illegal.
Green campaigners say that the very point of protest is to cause disruption and that Extinction Rebellion’s action over the past couple of years forced the government to adopt radical climate change targets, such as committing to making the UK net-zero by 2050.
Police will not need the new laws to prosecute those found guilty of violence in Bristol last night, but the government says that Patel’s bill will give the police the power to stop the kind of violence perpetrated in Bristol earlier in the day.
A Home Office source said: “Clearly most of the events that we saw at the weekend are likely to be prosecuted under existing legislation anyway, but it’s obviously being able to have the sensible interventions at an early enough stage before it becomes a full-blown riot.”
Opponents of the bill admit that the riots in Bristol will hurt their attempts to stop it. “There is a debate to be had and there’s debate to be had about all proposed government legislation,” said Marvin Rees, the mayor of Bristol. “But I think there are particular concerns about this bill and we’ll speak about those more on another occasion.
“But the violence that happened in a city last night goes nowhere to actually reducing the likelihood of this bill winning support. In fact, it does quite the contrary. People from those communities who have been on the rough end of the criminal justice system are now in more danger. It doesn’t put them closer to justice, it puts them further away.
“It runs absolutely against what they claim to be in fighting for — political illiteracy at large.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Law in a Time of Crisis by Jonathan Sumption, review — the celebrity judge takes aim at Brexit and lockdown
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Judges used to be household names. Lord Denning, never publicity shy, once appeared on Wogan alongside the singer Ian Dury, and the chat show regular Judge James Pickles had his own column in The Sun.
The law is more self-effacing these days, but Jonathan Sumption has become something of a celebrity, partly because of his outspoken opposition to lockdown.
The retired Supreme Court judge is a former Oxford history don, the author of a series of books about the Hundred Years’ War. He is a linguist who speaks fluent French and Italian and reads Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, Dutch and Latin. He is a music lover who sits on the board of English National Opera. As a polymath, he is Jonathan Miller in a horsehair wig.
Law in a Time of Crisis is an edited collection of lectures, and on reading them you might find it difficult to tell whether he is a historian who happens to be a lawyer or a lawyer with an exaggerated sense of history.
What is not in doubt is the fluency of his writing. He is lively and entertaining on even the most arcane of subjects. “Never underestimate the importance of entertainment as a tool of advocacy,” he writes. He certainly has a colourful turn of phrase, noting at one point that “Pride and Prejudice is in a sense a prolonged commentary on the law of entailed land”.
For the most part his arguments are interesting enough even without the additional colour. In one lecture he suggests that Magna Carta is overrated. “Far from it being a blueprint for future constitutional development,” he writes, “Magna Carta was really the last gasp of the old order.”
The Magna Carta myth, he suggests, was largely invented in the 17th century by the leading lawyer of the day, Edward Coke, to annoy the Stuart kings.
There are two lectures about Brexit, one a very balanced summary that was first delivered to an audience of German judges. Sumption, who voted to stay in the EU, is so balanced, in fact, that he dismisses John Bercow as “rude, loud and excessively talkative”, but praises the way the former Speaker adapted parliament to cope with the problems of minority government.
He also compares Boris Johnson to Disraeli, whom he describes as “an outsider, an ambitious adventurer and an unscrupulous opportunist . . . totally amoral . . . and, as it turned out, an excellent prime minister”.
In Sumption’s view the 2016 referendum was the wrong tool for deciding Brexit because voters could not take a view on our future relations with the European Union. Yet he appears to support the Scottish referendum. Did this not also fail to take into account future relations with the United Kingdom?
In a chapter on diversity among judges he notes that 67 per cent of French judges are women (apparently French men just don’t fancy the job) and suggests that British judges would be more diverse if they were still picked by the lord chancellor, as used to be the case.
Writing about secrecy in government, he argues that attempts to create more open government have led to more secrecy. Conducting an informal survey of retired civil servants, he discovered that almost all of them had omitted key information from internal documents, recording more sensitive points on Post-it Notes that were later destroyed.
His harshest words are directed at the government’s lockdown policy. “I believe that history will look back on the measures taken . . . as a monument of collective hysteria and government folly.”
Sumption is strong on evidence and logic, but is perhaps weaker on politics. He easily picks apart the fashion for apologising for the sins of the past, which he describes as “morally worthless”, but is there anybody who believes that the apologies are sincere? They’re surely a gesture designed to give a modern political message.
And in a section on the constitution he describes parliament as the “only institutional means by which the electorate can influence policy”. That’s accurate, but is it relevant? In the age of Black Lives Matter and Extinction Rebellion, parliament isn’t shaping opinion — it is struggling to keep up.
Law in a Time of Crisis by Jonathan SumptionProfile £16.99 pp240

https://www.thetimes.com/article/reclusi.title: Reclusive hedge fund boss takes home record £343m
https://www.thetimes.com/article/reclusi.subtitle: The son of car mechanic is rewarded for his hedge fund’s bumper year
https://www.thetimes.com/article/reclusi.text:
Even in a sector accustomed to generous salaries, Sir Chris Hohn’s pay packet is something remarkable.
The billionaire hedge fund manager has been paid a record £343 million after a bumper year for his Children’s Investment Fund.
The sum, equivalent to £940,000 a day, is believed to be the highest annual amount ever paid to an individual in Britain, beating the £323 million collected by Denise Coates, the boss of Bet365, the online bookmaker, in 2018.
According to a Companies House filing, Hohn, a former boss of Rishi Sunak, the chancellor, and a prominent value-based investment fund manager, collected the pay in dividends from TCI, the hedge fund he established in 2003, after a 66 per cent rise in pre-tax profits to £499 million.
The dividends, which equate to about 2,144 times the prime minister’s basic salary, were paid to his personal company, TCF Fund Management (UK).
The filing, for the year to February 29, 2020, shows that TCF Fund Management, which he owns outright, has total shareholder funds of almost $2 billion.
Hohn, from Surrey, is also known as one of Britain’s most generous philanthropists and in 2019 gave away $386 million (more than £270 million) through the Children’s Investment Fund Foundation, his personal charity. He has donated to projects tackling climate change and various children’s charities.
The son of a Jamaican car mechanic who came to Britain in the 1960s, Hohn graduated from Southampton University in 1988 with a first-class degree in accounting and business economics.
He worked at Apax Partners, a private equity group, and Perry Capital, an American hedge fund. He was made head of Perry’s London operation in 1998 and set up the Children’s Investment Fund in 2003. It has significant holdings in some of the world’s biggest companies, including Microsoft, Alphabet, the parent company of Google, and Visa.
Sunak was employed as junior analyst at the hedge fund between 2006 and 2009.
The latest filings underline how Hohn has continued to outperform fellow activist investors. He has long been one of Britain’s highest-paid people, after receiving £200 million in dividends in 2018.
Though reclusive, he is no stranger to controversy and was compared to a “locust” by a German regulator for his part in derailing Deutsche Börse’s 2005 bid for the London stock exchange. TCI, his hedge fund, is based in Mayfair but its ultimate parent company is based in the Cayman Islands, a tax haven.
Hohn donated £200,000 to Extinction Rebellion, the climate change campaign group, in 2019, saying that there was an “urgent need” for people to tackle the crisis.
He has encouraged asset managers to put more pressure on listed companies to act on climate change. He told the Financial Times that the asset management industry behaved like sheep and was a joke in respect of what they were “actually doing [with respect to climate change]”.
The Children’s Investment Fund was co-founded by Jamie Cooper, Hohn’s American former wife. In 2014 she was awarded £337 million in one of the biggest divorce awards made in the English courts.
Cooper expressed disappointment at the settlement, saying that she should get half of a £1 billion fortune because the wealth was created as a result of their partnership.
They subsequently had a dispute over Hohn’s charity, which resulted in him being ordered to pay £270 million to Cooper’s charity.
Hohn was knighted in 2014 for his philanthropy. According to The Sunday Times Rich List his fortune is estimated at £1.2 billion.
Payback time
Denise Coates — £323 million The previous record for the boss of a British company was held by Coates, the co-founder of Bet365. As joint chief executive and majority shareholder of the privately owned gambling site she paid herself a £277 million salary and about £46 million in dividends for 2018.
Bart Becht — £92 million Reckitt Benckiser, which makes Cillit Bang and Clearasil, paid its Dutch chief executive Becht £92 million in 2009, a figure that remains a record for a company listed in London.
Sir Martin Sorrell — £70.4 million WPP, the world’s biggest advertising company, triggered a backlash from shareholders when it paid Sorrell, the chief executive, more than £70 million in 2015, primarily due to huge long-term share bonuses. More than a third of investors voted against its pay policy.
Tim Steiner — £58.7 million The pay of Ocado’s co-founder for 2019 was swelled by a £54 million bonus under a long-term incentive scheme linked to the online grocery company’s share price.
Jeff Fairburn — £47.1 million The housebuilder Persimmon sparked outrage among investors with huge bonus payments to its executives in 2017 and 2018. Fairburn, the chief executive, received a total of £47.1 million in 2017 which led to a backlash that culminated in his exit in November 2018. He was paid a further £39 million for 2018.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: What caused the protest in Bristol and how it unfolded
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
No organiser Participants in the “Kill the Bill” event said that the lack of a single organiser meant that it was vulnerable to being hijacked by a violent minority. Groups that encouraged their followers to attend the protest included Extinction Rebellion, All Black Lives Bristol and Socialist Workers Party Bristol. Another, No Fixed Abode Anti Fascists, told people not to share footage of protesters unless they were in masks.
Marvin Rees, the mayor of Bristol, said that the riot had nothing to do with the “real everyday struggles” that people in the city face after 12 months of the pandemic. He said that it had been fuelled by those who “go around looking for the latest demo”. Avon and Somerset police issued an appeal for people not to attend, but Andy Marsh, the chief constable, said there was no “prior intelligence” of disorder planned “on this scale”.
Peaceful beginnings Until 5pm the protest had followed the pattern of previous peaceful demonstrations in the city. About 3,000 people opposed to a new law that would give police greater powers to curtail protests had converged on College Green at 2pm before marching a mile through the city centre to Castle Park.
Billy, 43, a musician, described the afternoon as “a typical peaceful Bristol protest” with chanting and placards. Jamie Leigh-Davies, 20, a student at Bristol University, said the march had “people of all ages and it was peaceful and people just having a good time”. She left the protest before it turned violent, but watched events unfold outside the police station. “It was a completely different group,” she said.
Man in the black bandana The crowd were listening to “uplifting speeches” and a poetry performance when a man wearing a mask made from a black bandana, urged people to march to the police headquarters at Bridewell Street. Billy recalled: “The guy popped up from the back of the crowd and shouted: ‘The police can’t hear you from here. You know where they can hear you? Yep, the police station, let’s go!’ In that split second one guy walked to the police station and a bunch of people followed.”
Violence breaks out By 6pm a section of the protesters who had been drinking alcohol were hurling bottles and cans at officers. Adaia Norris Witts, 20, a fine art student, said: “They were throwing bottles at about 6pm. About an hour and a half later we saw someone set the police van on fire and we were all screaming [for them to stop]. This was not the message we wanted to be conveyed.”
For the next four hours there was a steady ratcheting up of tension as rioters climbed on to the station and sprayed anti-police slurs, broke the station windows, threw projectiles at the lines of riot police and eventually set fire to vehicles. Xuankai Ng, 21, a law student at Bristol University, said: “I think people threw a box of fireworks inside the van and it exploded — there was a lot of smoke. The [police] car was on fire afterwards.”
By 9pm agitators were throwing anything they could find at police officers including pieces of scaffolding. In total, 21 officers were injured in what police described as the worst case of violent disorder in the city for a decade. Protesters stamped on one policeman, puncturing his lung, and fractured another officer’s arm.
The police reaction “It wasn’t a peaceful protest that suddenly erupted into a riot,” Billy said. “There were various things that happened but there was no real retaliation from the police.” The restraint shown by officers during the stand-off was captured when two women urinated at the feet of riot police.
The women were cheered on by the crowd as officers continued to hold their position to protect the station from being ransacked. Andy Roebuck, the chairman of Avon and Somerset Police Federation, said: “[Officers] said they felt they were going to be killed.”
History of Bristol Bristol has a rich history of protest dating back to the 18th century, although relatively few recent protests have been violent. On June 7, 2020, an otherwise peaceful rally toppled a statue of Edward Colston because of his links to the slave trade and cast it into the harbour.
The most recent outbreak of violence was in August 2011, prompted by riots in London that began when police shot dead Mark Duggan, a 29-year-old black man.
Previous riots include the race riots in the St Paul’s district in the 1980s, the Queens Square Reform riots of 1831 and the Bristol Bridge riots of 1793.

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.title: Stroud is named best place to live in the UK 2021
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.text:
Saturday morning in Stroud is always a spectacle, and last weekend was no exception. Families queued at stalls selling doughnuts, the smell of Thai food filled the air and a lone woman strode past carrying a large piece of cardboard bearing the words “stop racism”. In every direction beautiful wooded hills appeared through gaps between buildings, while on the restored canal, a dog in a life jacket floated past on a paddleboard.
“There are all sorts of things going on here, but everyone has the aim of keeping Stroud independent and local,” says Dominic Salter. A Stroudie for 30 years, he is typical of this former industrial town where adaptability, innovation and local pride are the norm. Salter is one of the bosses of the award-winning Salt Bakehouse, which responded instantly to the pandemic, delivering its bread, pastries and “scruffins” (made with rolled-up croissant dough stuffed with custard, £2.50) by ebike, and converting a van into a mobile shop to tour the surrounding villages.
Stroud is independent and lively, but it also has the basics covered. The schools are excellent, as are the transport links and the surrounding Cotswold countryside. Take a walk on one of the commons — Minchinhampton, Rodborough, Selsley — or hike five miles to Coaley Peak for stunning views of the Severn Vale.
Novelist Jilly Cooper has lived in Stroud for nearly 40 years. Prolific as ever, her latest book, Between the Covers, is a collection of columns she wrote for The Sunday Times 50 years ago. She has also written a book about football, which is due to be published next year.
Cooper says: “It’s so beautiful here and it’s such an inspiring area to write about. These incredible valleys are carpeted with green grass, often with a stream at the bottom and mighty trees higher up. There’s wonderful wildlife — we get foxes and deer in the garden. The stone of the houses is like a mirror: grey on grey days, shiny when the sun’s out and glowing red at sunset.
“It’s incredibly friendly. It’s great dog-walking country and everyone gets on with everyone else. We’ve got lovely pubs, a fantastic vet and a village shop that really looks after us.”
It is this friendly spirit that attracted Dale Vince, new-age traveller turned green energy pioneer and owner of Ecotricity. He says: “The people are brilliant and there’s a real creative and alternative scene. And I really like the fact that it’s an industrial, working town surrounded by all this lush countryside.”
As well as owning Ecotricity, the town’s biggest employer, he’s chairman of the local football team, Forest Green Rovers (Cooper is a big fan), just down the road in Nailsworth. Their bright green shirts, vegan fare and wooden stadium are perfect symbols of the eco-tinged unconventionality that’s a big part of Stroud’s charm.
The star attraction is the farmers’ market on Saturdays. With more than 50 stalls, it’s one of the biggest and best in the country. It’s not the only game in town, though. At the Jolly Nice farm shop just outside Stroud you can get the best local produce — fruit and veg, rare-breed beef — seven days a week. Ingeniously, it has turned itself into a drive-through during the pandemic.
The town centre is a bit on the scruffy side with some vacant shops, although it is improving. The nearly revamped Five Valleys Shopping Centre is also taking shape, with a smart department store in Sandersons Boutique due to open next month and an artisan food market adding welcome character alongside Halfords and Poundland.
Extinction Rebellion was founded here, and you’re never far from a plastic-free shop or a wholefoods store. Woodruffs, which claims to be Britain’s first organic café, is still going strong; its vegetarian “shepherd’s pie” (£7) is among dishes available for takeaway or local delivery. The big annual event is the Stroud Wassail, when morris dancers and mummers gather to wish Stroudies and visitors a successful new year in semi-pagan style.
There’s usually an interesting exhibition or poetry event at the Stroud Valleys Artspace, and when nights out are allowed again you’re guaranteed a good one at the Sub Rooms, a home of gigs and theatre (the James Taylor Quartet and a stage version of Horrible Histories have been pencilled in for the summer), or the Stroud Brewery bar, where you can wash down a New Age Hippy vegan pizza (£11) with a pint of Big Cat stout — all organic and, as they say, “very Stroud”.
You like independent spirit in well-connected Cotswold countryside.
It’s one of the contradictions of Stroud that many of the people who say they love it choose to live in a village on one of the commons, rather than in the town itself. The most expensive and sought-after houses are in Rodborough (very much part of Stroud) and Minchinhampton (further out).
There are direct trains to Cheltenham (from 35 minutes), Swindon (from 28 minutes) and London Paddington (from 1 hour 26 minutes). By car it’s a 30-minute drive north to Cheltenham or Gloucester and 20 minutes west to the M5, then 35 minutes south to Bristol.
Central Stroud, ie near the River Frome and the Stroudwater Navigation canal, has a high number of slow spots — the town has good superfast coverage otherwise. Outlying villages have full fibre networks built by Gigaclear, so should have good speeds.
The two selective grammars, Stroud High School (inspected in 2010) and Marling School (2013, both for ages 11 to 18), are rated outstanding by Ofsted and feature in The Sunday Times Parent Power guide, as do Rodborough Community Primary School and Hopelands Preparatory School (from £2,200 per term).
No problems.
A walk on Rodborough Common. Enjoy the views then reward yourself with a scoop of banana and toffee ripple from Winstones ice cream parlour — they now deliver (22 flavours, including three vegan options, from £4.20 per litre).
The radicalism sometimes goes a bit too far: the Beacon, a community hub where concerned locals have gathered to discuss the “health risks” of the 5G phone network, was criticised by a doctor for its poster questioning the seriousness of the pandemic.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Longer jail terms don’t stop crime, admits Chris Philp, justice minister
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
A justice minister has admitted there is little evidence that longer sentences help to cut crime, despite his own department introducing laws yesterday to increase jail terms.
Chris Philp, the minister responsible for sentencing, said that detailed research had found that the likelihood of being caught and punished was much more important in discouraging people from committing crime than the length of jail sentences.
Answering a parliamentary question about the deterrent effect of longer sentences, he said: “The evidence is mixed, although harsher sentencing tends to be associated with limited or no general deterrent effect. Increases in the certainty of apprehension and punishment have consistently been found to have a deterrent effect.”
The comments from Philp, who is also the minister in charge of immigration compliance, put him at odds with measures in the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Bill that will impose longer sentences for a variety of offences.
While many of the sentencing changes are intended to lengthen jail terms for serious sexual and violent offences, there are also changes to lower level crimes. The maximum penalty for criminal damage of a memorial or statue is to be increased from three months to ten years. The bill will also increase the maximum sentence for breaching the conditions police impose on protests from three to six months in an attempt to crack down on disruptive tactics from radical groups such as Extinction Rebellion.
Separate legislation to be introduced later in the year will increase the maximum sentence for people smuggling from 14 years to life.
The Ministry of Justice insisted that its increased sentences were meant to protect the public and punish perpetrators rather than act as deterrents. A source from the ministry said: “Sentencing isn’t all about deterrence. People who are in prison don’t pose a threat to the public and a strong punitive element to sentencing is crucial in maintaining public confidence in the criminal justice system.”
Prison reform campaigners welcomed Philp’s comments and questioned why his department was going ahead with its plans for longer sentences, which they argued would only place further pressure on Britain’s creaking prisons system.
Peter Dawson, director of the Prison Reform Trust, said: “With prisons in the grip of an unprecedented operational crisis, this bill will make it even less likely that they will achieve the standards of decency and humanity to which the government claims to be committed.”
Frances Crook, chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said: “Everyone wants to see less crime, but even the Ministry of Justice’s own research has shown that this will not be achieved by making sentences longer.”
Robert Buckland, the justice secretary, has defended the changes and insisted that the tougher sentences at the top end would be balanced with “smarter ones at the lower end”.
He told Sky News: “The most important functions of our prisons system is indeed public protection and we need to emphasise that. But at the same time there are a whole raft of initiatives we’re taking with regards to rehabilitation of offenders.”
A government spokesman said: “We make no apologies for prioritising public protection by ensuring serious and dangerous offenders are off our streets for longer. At the same time, our 20,000 extra police will help to deter criminals and significantly reduce their chances of evading justice.”
